speakingSourceEnglish: Chat with a fellow guest: say what you eat for breakfast, ask if they drink coffee or tea, and ask if they live here.
speakingObjectives: Chat with a fellow guest and say what you eat for breakfast, for example: « Je mange des chilaquiles au petit-déjeuner. »
Say what you drink, for example: « Je bois du café. »
Ask whether they drink coffee or tea, with tu as in card 12 and Reader line 5: « Tu bois du café ou du thé ? »
Ask whether they live here: « Tu habites ici ? » with a fellow guest your age (Reader line 7 model), or « Vous habitez ici ? » with someone you address formally (card 13 model).
Use tu with a fellow guest your age; use vous with staff or with someone you address formally.
sourceNotes: Source English card and Reader text is copied unedited into packet english fields, forms.englishPrompt and modes.modelEnglish, mapped by 1-based index.

Food terms: only chilaquiles is kept as a named dish. The Spanish words left in the candidate were replaced with French terms that teach the meaning directly: œufs au plat (fried eggs), haricots (beans), bacon, sauce verte (green salsa), avocat (avocado), porridge (oatmeal). This affects cards 3, 4, 7, 8, 9, 10 and 14 and Reader lines 1, 3, 6, 8 and 9.
Setting and names: Oaxaca and Puebla are kept, Lucía keeps her source spelling, and the Reader title is supplied in readerTitleFrench.

Register: the source contrast is preserved. Card 12 and Reader lines 5 and 7 follow source tú with tu; card 13 follows source usted with vous; card 16 follows source ustedes with plural vous addressed to staff. The candidate's blanket vous and its claim that polite fr-FR was required were removed, because the source says to use tú with a fellow guest your age.

Source register tension (flagged, not edited): card 13 and its note teach formal '¿Usted vive aquí?' for someone you just met, while Reader line 7 has Emma ask the same question of the same fellow guest with tú ('¿Tú vives aquí en Oaxaca?'). The French mirrors each item as written: vous on card 13, tu in Reader line 7. The speaking objectives name which model each phrasing follows.

Paradigm gap, Spanish versus French: the source focus is the regular present tense of three Spanish classes, -ar (desayunar, tomar), -er (comer) and -ir (vivir), for yo, tú, usted, nosotros and ellos. These classes do not map onto French conjugation groups. In this lesson only manger and habiter are regular French verbs, and both are first-group -er verbs: je mange, tu manges, il/elle mange, nous mangeons (spelling change), vous mangez, ils/elles mangent; j'habite, tu habites, il/elle habite, nous habitons, vous habitez, ils/elles habitent.

Paradigm gap, irregular French counterparts: desayunar becomes the phrase prendre son petit-déjeuner and tomar becomes boire, both irregular. They are taught as lexical items: je prends, tu prends, il/elle prend, nous prenons, vous prenez, ils/elles prennent; je bois, tu bois, il/elle boit, nous buvons, vous buvez, ils/elles boivent. Vivir is rendered with habiter because vivre is irregular. French does have regular -ir verbs (second group, such as finir and choisir), but none occurs in this lesson. The source -ir example abrir (card 16) is rendered with être ouvert, so it does not model an -ir verb either.

Paradigm gap, pronouns: French requires subject pronouns where Spanish usually drops them. Spanish usted and ustedes take third-person verb forms, while French vous has its own second-person plural form and covers both formal singular and plural address. The French therefore cannot reproduce the source's three-class ending contrast or the -emos/-imos ending distinction.

Forms: six full Reader pairs in Reader order (lines 2, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8). Each is labelled as regular or irregular in its note; irregular prendre and boire lines are included as marked lexical items, not as models of regular endings.

Modes: six unique modes (see, recall, hear, type, say, write). Each promptFrench is the exact French card or Reader text and each targetEnglish is the exact source English. Cards 12 and 13 are both included so the tu and vous contrast is exercised. The hear mode has no audio attached.
Naturalness fixes: card 11 and Reader line 2 use 'Je prends mon petit-déjeuner'; card 16 is 'Vous êtes ouverts le dimanche ?' with singular le for a habitual day.
Typography: a no-break space (U+00A0) precedes each colon and sits inside guillemets, and a narrow no-break space (U+202F) precedes each question mark; both are written as JSON escapes.
qualifiedReviewResiduals: Private, unreviewed draft: no qualified approval, no audio attached, and no claim of learner readiness.
No vous form occurs in the Reader, so the forms list (Reader pairs only) has no usted/vous example; vous appears only on cards 13 and 16.
No regular French -ir verb appears, so the source -ir grammar point has no French counterpart in this lesson.
Irregular prendre, boire, mettre and être appear in card and Reader text; a qualified reviewer should judge whether that fits beginner pacing.

Lexical choices to confirm with a qualified French reviewer: 'le bacon' versus 'le lard' or 'la poitrine fumée' for Mexican tocino; 'le porridge' versus 'les flocons d'avoine' for avena; 'la sauce verte' versus keeping 'salsa verte'; plain 'haricots' versus 'haricots noirs' or 'haricots rouges'.
The card 13 versus Reader line 7 register tension lies in the immutable source and remains unresolved; the French only mirrors it and flags it.
All French is an unreviewed AI candidate; qualified French/domain review is required. The model triad is not approval.
No audio is attached to this candidate. Any earlier audio recorded for different exact text is invalid for these revised French strings.
Owner-only review is a candidate disposition, not learner registration or progress activation.

Spanish source drills regular -ar/-er/-ir present forms, whereas exact English and French Reader introduce irregular French verbs and no regular -ir form. Progression needs qualified editorial review.
Speaking objective “say what you drink” is supplemental to the source speaking task but drawn from the source lesson objective (“what you eat and drink”).

The pinned Spanish Reader carries 4 full verb paradigms (desayunar, tomar, comer, vivir); this packet preserves them as source evidence but has no authored full French verb paradigms. The verb progression gap must be shown explicitly in owner review and resolved before learner release.
projectionStatus: conditional owner-only review only if source register/salsa caveats and missing French full verb paradigms are shown; learner gates closed
internalDomainNotes: Fable described chilaquiles as fried tortilla pieces with red or green sauce and a classic Mexican breakfast; verify with a qualified Mexican-food reviewer before learner use.
Fable suggested black or red beans as a Mexican specification; the source only says beans, so neither color is added to the learner card.
The Mexican salsa verde versus French sauce verte equivalence requires food-language review; this is marked on card 8.
The source Reader line about eating beans in Puebla may imply local distinctiveness; preserve the source without editorial embellishment and ask a qualified domain reviewer.
